children: is preparing to make one of its most pivotal decisions since becoming an independent company, Bloomberg reported Thursday: whether to take the world's biggest platinum mine underground.
The Mogalakwena asset in South Africa’s Limpopo province is the former Anglo American unit's flagship operation, with more than 80 years of reserves remaining, but Valterra
has been exploring beneath the surface as ore grades in the open pits decline, and the company plans to reach a final investment decision on the expansion next year.
"We believe that going underground is the most cost-effective option for us," Valterra
CFO Sayurie Naidoo said in an interview with Bloomberg.
If approved, the Sandsloot underground project would unlock millions of ounces of high-grade ore at a time when global output of platinum group metals is expected to dwindle.

owns three operations in South Africa, which holds nearly 80% of global reserves of platinum group metals, but the evolution of Mogalakwena would be a vote of confidence from an industry that has been concerned about the uncertainty of future demand as the biggest source of consumption—devices that reduce harmful emissions from gasoline and diesel cars—is under pressure from the rise of electric vehicles.
"We have many, many decades of PGMs available just within our portfolio, so the supply is not a concern," CEO Craig Miller said in the interview.

title: Valterra nears decision to dig underground at world's largest platinum mine
